blocks.text: Week in wildlife: a friendly seal, a furious goldcrest and ‘the swanfather’
This week’s best wildlife photographs from around the world

blocks.alt: An elephant seal appears to wavet o beachgoers as it pops by the shore of Copacabana Beach in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil

Angry bird by Jan Wittmer is one of the winners of the Comedy Wildlife awards 2026. Wittmer said: ‘During my photo trip to the island of Helgoland, Germany, I encountered a goldcrest for the first time – and it was love at first sight. Europe’s smallest bird wandered right in front of me, presumably searching for food. To get a perspective at eye level, I placed my camera on the ground. My heart was pounding and my finger was glued to the shutter as the tiny bird darted back and forth. Suddenly, it came to a stop and looked straight at the camera

blocks.alt: A stag bellows during the rutting season in Bushy Park, London, UK

ABengal tiger tigress with cubs in Ranthambhore, India. Nature is in “freefall” across the world, but recoveries in species from tigers to tuna provide hope for reversing declines, conservationists have said. Conservation charity WWF has unveiled its latest Living Planet report, which shows that wildlife populations have declined globally by nearly three-quarters since 1970

blocks.text: Living Planet report , the World Wildlife Fund writes: “In 2010, only around 3,200 wild tigers remained, and the species seemed to be sliding toward extinction. By 2025, the population had grown to roughly 5,700, an increase of more than 70%”Photograph: Andy Rouse/WWF/PA

blocks.alt: An American bullfrog floats in a cattle watering trough as a tiny insect crawls across its face on a ranch in rural southwestern Oregon, US. Native to central and eastern North America, bullfrogs are invasive in Oregon, where they compete with and prey on native wildlife, including amphibians, fish and turtles
Egrets stand tall in front of a wind power plant in the background in Mannar, Sri Lanka
A golden jackal spots the photographer in Kocacay Delta in Bursa, Turkey

A wētāpunga, the world’s heaviest insect in New Zealand. The population the endemic insect is officially increasing thanks to a groundbreaking breeding programme that has overseen the release of 11,000 insects into the wild

blocks.text: wētāpunga , the world’s heaviest insect, in New Zealand. The flightless cricket, which can be up to 10cm (4in) long, used to be found across the North Island, but by the 1990s had retreated to a few smaller islands. However, a new breeding programme has released 11,000 wētāpunga into the wild – grounds for hope for the species’ futurePhotograph: Anton Sorokin/Alamy

blocks.alt: Steve Platt, also known as the “the swan father” chases a black swan during the 46th annual swan round on Lake Morton, Florida, US. City officials roundup the swans for their annual medical checkups

A cockscomb during harvesting on the outskirts of Srinagar, Jammu and Kashmir, India. Locally known as ‘Mawal,’ the vibrant annual flower is prized for both its ornamental beauty and culinary uses. Its crimson blooms are traditionally hand-harvested, sun-dried, and ground into a fine powder, serving as a natural, chemical-free food coloring in traditional Kashmiri cuisine, most notably in iconic Wazwan feast dishes such as Rogan Josh

Visitors photograph wild bison crossing a road at Grand Teton National Park in Wyoming, US. The park’s bison belong to the free-ranging Jackson herd, which summers in Grand Teton and winters on the adjacent National Elk Refuge
A ladybird takes off from a autumn colored leaf in a city park in Tallinn, Estonia
An Arabian sand gazelle walks in the sand dunes in the Dubai suburbs, UAE

A flamingo flies across Kocacay Delta in Bursa, Turkey. The delta, characterised by extensive wetlands, marshes, shallow waters, and floodplain ecosystems, hosts rich biodiversity by providing vital feeding, shelter, and breeding habitats for numerous bird and mammal species

Visitors watch the shark still trapped in an artificial waterway in the southeastern port city of Busa, South Korea. Coast guard boats have made several attempts to guide it back to the sea but so far they have failed

Parrots seized along with another 377 live exotic animals at the port of Pozzallo, Sicily, Italy. Police and customs intercepted an illicit transport of 300 tortoises and 77 parrots, carried out by a Maltese citizen, during an inspection carried out near the boarding point for the catamaran bound for Malta

blocks.text: parrots were seized by customs staff at the port of Pozzallo, Sicily, Italy. They were found in a car about to board a catamaran bound for Malta. The driver of the car, rather ambitiously, had hoped to smuggle out 300 tortoises and 77 parrots, many of which were protected species. The animals are now in the care of a breeding facilityPhotograph: Guardia Di Finanza - Ragusa

A bee collects pollen in the sunshine in Dunsden, UK
